Years 11–13 Technology

Learning expectations
Through Technology, students are taught that effective and ethical design respects the unique
relationship between people and their physical environment, and embraces the significance of
culture and world views in technological practice and innovation.

The learning area supports students to be innovative, reflective, and critical in designing new
models, products, software, systems, and tools to benefit people while taking account of their
impact on cultural, ethical, environmental, and economic conditions.


Key features of the refreshed learning area
•   Clear progression from Years 9–10 through to advanced Technology pathways.
•   Explicit teaching of disciplinary writing and communication so students can explain processes,
    interpret evidence, and justify design, material, production, and technical decisions.
•   Greater visibility of responsible practice, including cultural, ethical, environmental, social,
    privacy, safety, and sustainability considerations.
•   Strong connections between disciplinary knowledge and practical application through
    designing, making, processing, constructing, testing, evaluating, and refining outcomes.
•   Clear progression in practical and technical skills, including the safe and purposeful use of
    materials, tools, equipment, processes, and production methods.
•   Authentic contexts that connect learning with industry, science, engineering, creative practice,
    community needs, and environmental challenges.
•   Specialist pathways that support students with different interests, strengths, and future
    aspirations.


Subjects
Subjects within the Technology learning area are:

•   Years 11–13 Food Processing Technology
•   Years 11–13 Resistant Materials Technology
•   Years 11–13 Textiles Technology
•   Years 11–13 Spatial and Product Design.

Learning and pathways

Years 11–13 Food Processing Technology
Students are taught food science concepts from biotechnology, chemistry, microbiology, and
nutrition. They apply this knowledge to the development of food products through human-centred
design, systems thinking, food safety, sustainability, and consideration of consumer needs.

Strands

Years 11–13 Food Processing Technology is organised into four strands:

•   Food Fundamentals
•   Food Sustainability
•   Food Innovation
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Programme design

Programmes should integrate knowledge and practices from across the Food Processing
Technology strands through the practical development, testing, refinement, and evaluation of food-
related outcomes. Contexts and products can vary, but they should provide sufficient scope for
students to apply the prescribed knowledge and practices and demonstrate the expected level of
complexity for the year level.

Pathways

Years 11– 13 Food Processing Technology leads to pathways in food process engineering, food
science, food technology, product design, hospitality, biotechnology, and health.

Years 11–13 Resistant Materials Technology
Students are taught to apply knowledge of materials, manufacturing processes, and engineering
principles to design and construct functional products that meet identified needs and specifications.
They are taught how material properties, technological developments, user requirements,
environmental considerations, and production processes influence design decisions, product
performance, and the development of engineered outcomes.

Strands

Years 11–13 Resistant Materials Technology is organised into four strands:

•   Development of Technologies, Materials, and Manufacturing
•   Technical Design and Informed Decision-Making
•   Engineered Outcomes
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Programme design

Programmes should connect learning across the strands and provide sustained opportunities to
develop workshop capability through materials processing, construction, assembly, testing, quality
assurance, and refinement. Contexts and outcomes may vary, but they should allow students to
apply knowledge and practical skills at the expected level of technical complexity. Knowledge and
practices may be drawn together through one or more Resistant Materials Technology contexts. A
context provides a vehicle for learning and does not prescribe a single year-long project.

Pathways

Resistant Materials Technology leads to pathways in industrial design, product design,
engineering, manufacturing, and other industry pathways.

Years 11–13 Textiles Technology
Students are taught to apply textile materials and processes using an iterative user-centred design
framework to develop sustainable and fit-for-purpose outcomes. They examine how
anthropometric and dimensional data, material properties, stakeholder requirements, and ethical
and environmental considerations inform the design, development, evaluation, and refinement of
textile outcomes.

Strands

Years 11–13 Textiles Technology is organised into five strands:

•   Anthropometrics and Dimensional Data for Textile Design
•   Sustainable Responsibility and Ethical Practices
•   Technological Design Process in the Development of Textiles
•   Material Properties in Textiles
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Programme design

Programmes should integrate knowledge and practices from across the Textiles Technology
strands through the practical design, construction, treatment, finishing, testing, refinement, and
evaluation of textile outcomes. Projects may involve wearable or non-wearable textile outcomes
and should provide sufficient scope for students to develop practical textile skills, apply material
knowledge, and make informed design and construction decisions.

Pathways

Year 11–13 Textiles Technology leads to careers in material engineering and textile development,
fashion, commercial and residential interiors, and design and industry pathways.

Year 11–13 Spatial and Product Design
Students are taught how design outcomes emerge from the interaction of people, materials,
environments, and ideas. They are taught to analyse and respond to design opportunities using

creative and critical thinking, while considering how cultural, social, environmental, and contextual
factors influence design decisions and outcomes.

Strands

Years 11–13 Spatial and Product Design is organised into four strands:

•   Context and Precedents
•   Design Thinking Practices
•   Visual Communication
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Programme design

Programmes should integrate learning across Context and Precedents, Design Thinking Practices,
and Visual Communication. Students should be explicitly taught relevant knowledge of design
cultures, precedents, design elements and principles, human experience, materials, environments,
and visual communication conventions. This knowledge should be applied through spatial or
product design contexts that provide opportunities to generate, communicate, test, and refine
design ideas. Programmes should provide an appropriate balance of spatial and product design
learning and include the required studies of designers and design practices at each year level.

Pathways

Years 11–13 Spatial and Product Design leads to pathways in architecture, industrial and product
design, interior and spatial design, engineering, and related creative and technological disciplines.


How to design a programme
•   The knowledge and practice statements within each element are related, but teachers may
    select complementary statements from across strands and elements to support coherence and
    depth within a project. Disciplinary writing is most effectively taught when integrated across the
    teaching programme.
•   Technology subjects are inherently project-based, with projects providing contexts for students
    to apply, connect, and demonstrate prescribed knowledge and practices. Projects should be
    appropriately scoped to support explicit teaching, technical and practical skill development,
    informed decision-making, testing, refining, and evaluation.


Connections to other learning areas
Technology connects strongly with:

•   Science through material properties, food science, microbiology, measurement, forces,
    modelling, experimentation, and evidence from testing
•   Mathematics and Statistics through measurement, scale, geometry, calculation, modelling,
    data interpretation, tolerances, and quantitative evaluation

•   English through disciplinary writing, technical communication, explanation, evaluation, and
    evidence-based justification
•   Social Sciences through the cultural, social, ethical, economic, and societal implications of
    technological development
•   Health and Physical Education through hauora, food and nutrition, ergonomics, accessibility,
    safety, and the effects of technological outcomes on people and communities
•   The Arts through visual communication, composition, aesthetics, storytelling, interaction, and
    creative practice
•   Commerce through product development, enterprise, manufacturing, consumer needs, cost,
    market considerations, and commercial decision-making.
These Technology subjects also connect with Digital Technologies, Computer Science, Digital
Media, and Electronics and Mechatronics, through shared knowledge and practices relating to
design, digital tools and systems, technical development, testing, refinements, responsible
practice, and evaluation. These subjects are described in the Years 11–13 Technology – Digital
Information Sheet.
